1.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

1.q: ק֤וּמִי וּ⁠לְכִי֙ אתי וּ⁠בֵיתֵ֔⁠ךְ וְ⁠ג֖וּרִי בַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֣ר תָּג֑וּרִי כִּֽי־קָרָ֤א יְהוָה֙ לָֽ⁠רָעָ֔ב וְ⁠גַם־בָּ֥א אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ שֶׁ֥בַע שָׁנִֽים
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since Yahweh has called for a famine, and also it will come upon the land seven years, arise and go, you and your house, and sojourn in where you will sojourn]
To translate the term **Arise** here and the term “arose” in the next verse, see how you translated the similar expression in 1:3. Alternate translation: [Take action and go]

Elisha is speaking as if the woman’s family were actually her **house**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [and your household] or [and your family]
It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [and sojourn where you can]

Elisha is using **has called for** as a common expression of his culture to mean “has determined that there will be.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has determined that there is going to be a famine]

2.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:7. Alternate translation: [what the man of God had said]

3.note: The author is using this phrase to introduce a new development within this event. See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:9, which also introduces a new development.

The author is using **to cry out to the king** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to make a formal appeal to the king” or “to petition the king.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to appeal to the king]

4.note: The king is using the adjective **great** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. The ULT shows that by supplying the word **things**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent word or phrase. Alternate translation: [the wonders]

5.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:9.
Gehazi is referring to the king by a respectful title. Use a comparable title or expression for addressing someone respectfully in your language. Alternate translation: [Sire]

6.note: While the expression **Return** is an imperative, this was not a command that the eunuch was capable of obeying. He did not possess the woman’s house and land. Instead, it describes what the king wanted the eunuch to accomplish. Alternate translation: [Make sure that she gets back everything that belonged to her]

7.note: The author is using this travel notice to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event. Alternate translation: [Sometime after this, Elisha made a trip to Damascus]

The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **was declared** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And someone declared to him]

8.note: To translate the term **hand** here and in the next verse, see how you translated the similar expression in 5:5. Alternate translation: [with you]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [asking whether I will live from this sickness.]

9.note: This phrase expresses a single idea. The expression **every good thing** tells what this **gift** consisted of. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [a gift consisting of every good thing of Damascus]

The author is saying **every** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and a wide range of good things from Damascus]

The author is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. The ULT shows that by supplying the word **thing**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent word or phrase. Alternate translation: [fine product of Damascus] or [luxury of Damascus]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:14. Alternate translation: [in his presence]

By calling himself **Your son**, the king is addressing Elisha respectfully. (This is equivalent to the way the king of Israel addressed him as “my father” in 6:21.) Use a comparable expression for addressing someone respectfully in your language.
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [to ask whether he will revive from this sickness]

10.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [tell him that reviving, he will revive]

Elisha is repeating forms of the verbs **revive** and **die** in order to intensify his expression of the ideas that they convey. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [He will certainly recover … he will certainly die]

11.note: Here, Elisha’s **face** represents the direction in which he was looking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And he looked steadily in one direction] or [And he fixed a stare]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he set his gaze upon Hazael until Hazael felt ashamed]

12.note: Even though Hazael is addressing Elisha directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **my lord** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [Why are you, my lord, weeping]

See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author and characters may speak of “the sons of” a person to mean the nation or tribe that consists of his descendants. Alternate translation: [to the Israelites]

Elisha is speaking as if Hazael will actually **send** these cities **into fire**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will set on fire] or [you will burn down]

13.q: כִּ֣י מָ֤ה עַבְדְּ⁠ךָ֙ הַ⁠כֶּ֔לֶב כִּ֣י יַעֲשֶׂ֔ה הַ⁠דָּבָ֥ר הַ⁠גָּד֖וֹל הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה
13.note: Hazael is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But your servant is merely a dog, so he will not do such a great thing!]

13.q: כִּ֣י מָ֤ה עַבְדְּ⁠ךָ֙ הַ⁠כֶּ֔לֶב כִּ֣י יַעֲשֶׂ֔ה
13.note: Hazael is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [But what am I, your servant, a dog, that I should do]

Hazael is speaking as if he were actually a **dog**. In this culture, dogs were wild, and people considered them dirty and regarded them with contempt. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is a contemptible person like your servant]

14.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [He told me that reviving, you would revive]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:10. Alternate translation: [You will certainly revive]

15.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Hazael, while the pronoun **his** refers to Ben Hadad. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that Hazael took a cloth … and spread it over Ben Hadad’s face]

16.q: וּ⁠בִ⁠שְׁנַ֣ת חָמֵ֗שׁ לְ⁠יוֹרָ֤ם בֶּן־אַחְאָב֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וִ⁠יהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה מָלַ֛ךְ יְהוֹרָ֥ם בֶּן־יְהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה
16.note: In this verse and the next two verses, the author is introducing **Jehoram** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Judah**. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar expressions in 1:17.

See the discussion of these names in the introduction to this chapter. The author sometimes calls the **son of Ahab** who succeeded him as king of Israel by the name Joram, as he does here, but sometimes he calls him Jehoram. Similarly, the author sometimes calls the **son of Jehoshaphat** who succeeded him as king of Judah by the name Jehoram, as he does here, but sometimes he calls him Joram.

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. (He is referring to the co-regency that Jehoram had had with his father Jehoshaphat for the previous seven years. See the discussion of this in the introduction to this chapter.) You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [after Jehoshaphat had been the king of Judah together with his son for seven years]

17.note: See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author says that a person was “a son of” a certain number of years in order to mean that the person was that many years old. Alternate translation: [He was 32 years old]

18.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֜לֶךְ בְּ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ ׀ מַלְכֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָשׂוּ֙ בֵּ֣ית אַחְאָ֔ב כִּ֚י בַּת־אַחְאָ֔ב הָֽיְתָה־לּ֖⁠וֹ לְ⁠אִשָּׁ֑ה
18.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since the daughter of Ahab was a wife to him, he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab did]

18.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֜לֶךְ בְּ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ ׀ מַלְכֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָשׂוּ֙ בֵּ֣ית אַחְאָ֔ב
18.note: See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author and characters often speak of how a person lived as if that were a way or path that the person **walked** along. Alternate translation: [And he lived as the kings of Israel had lived, doing just what the house of Ahab did]

See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author and characters may use the term “house” to mean the descendants of a king who ruled after him. Alternate translation: [the kings in the dynasty of Ahab]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:2. Alternate translation: [And he did what Yahweh considered to be evil]

19.note: Yahweh is using the image of a **lamp** to mean a continuing presence, just as the lamp that was kept burning in the sanctuary represented Yahweh’s continuing presence there. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to ensure that his descendants would have a continuing presence as kings]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:12. Alternate translation: [for his descendants]

The author is using the term **days** to mean time, since time is made up of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the time] or [perpetually]

20.note: The author is using the term **days** to refer to the time when Jehoram was ruling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [During the reign of Jehoram]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:10. Alternate translation: [the control of]

21.q: וַֽ⁠יְהִי־ה֞וּא קָ֣ם לַ֗יְלָה וַ⁠יַּכֶּ֨ה אֶת־אֱד֜וֹם הַ⁠סֹּבֵ֤יב אֵלָי⁠ו֙ וְ⁠אֵת֙ שָׂרֵ֣י הָ⁠רֶ֔כֶב
21.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that the Edomites had **surrounded** the king before the information that he **struck** them at **night**. You may also want to put the information about the **commanders of the chariotry** with the information that the king **struck** the Edomites. Alternate translation: [And the Edomites surrounded him, but it happened that he, he arose at night, and he and the commanders of the chariotry struck Edom]

The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he arose** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what the king did (he **struck Edom**) and what the people did (they **fled**). See how you translated the expression “he, he came” in 5:25, which similarly emphasizes a contrast. Alternate translation: [for his part, he arose]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [he took action]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [and he attacked]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:6. Alternate translation: [the Edomite army]
In this context, the term **people** refers to the soldiers in the Judean army. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but the soldiers fled to their tents]

The author is using **the people fled to its tents** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the soldiers stopped their military campaign altogether and each of them went back to his home and family. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 2 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 2 Samuel 18:17. Alternate translation: [but the rest of the soldiers abandoned the army and returned home]

22.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the sentence if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and it is still in rebellion to this day]
See how you translated the same expression in 2:22.

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could state the meaning in a way that would be natural. Alternate translation: [Libnah also rebelled at that time]

23.q: וְ⁠יֶ֛תֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י יוֹרָ֖ם וְ⁠כָל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֑ה הֲ⁠לֽוֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים לְ⁠מַלְכֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה
23.note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is concluding the story of Joram. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar phrases in 1:18.

24.note: The author is referring to death in a polite way by saying that Joram **lay down with his fathers**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [And Joram passed away] or [And Joram died]

See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author and characters often use the term “father” to mean “ancestor.” Alternate translation: [And Joram joined his ancestors in death] or [And Joram died, as his ancestors had died]

The expression **was buried** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people buried him in the same place where people had buried his ancestors]

25.q: בִּ⁠שְׁנַת֙ שְׁתֵּים־עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה לְ⁠יוֹרָ֥ם בֶּן־אַחְאָ֖ב מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל מָלַ֛ךְ אֲחַזְיָ֥הוּ בֶן־יְהוֹרָ֖ם מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה
25.note: In this verse and the next two verses, the author is introducing **Ahaziah** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Judah**. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar expressions in 8:16.

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **the year of 12**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the same expression in 1 Kings 15:1 and similar places in that book. Alternate translation: [In the twelfth year of Joram]

26.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:17. Alternate translation: [Ahaziah was 22 years old]
**Athaliah** was the daughter of Ahab, who was the son of **Omri**. Your language may have its own term or expression for this relationship. Alternate translation: [the grand-daughter of Omri]

27.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֗לֶךְ בְּ⁠דֶ֨רֶךְ֙ בֵּ֣ית אַחְאָ֔ב וַ⁠יַּ֧עַשׂ הָ⁠רַ֛ע בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה כְּ⁠בֵ֣ית אַחְאָ֑ב כִּ֛י חֲתַ֥ן בֵּית־אַחְאָ֖ב הֽוּא
27.note: The author is continuing to introduce Ahaziah. See how you translated the similar expressions in 8:18. Alternate translation: [And he lived as the kings who were descendants of Ahab had lived, and he did what Yahweh considered to be evil, just as the kings who were descendants of Ahab had done, for he was a son-in-law of the house of Ahab]

27.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֗לֶךְ בְּ⁠דֶ֨רֶךְ֙ בֵּ֣ית אַחְאָ֔ב וַ⁠יַּ֧עַשׂ הָ⁠רַ֛ע בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה כְּ⁠בֵ֣ית אַחְאָ֑ב כִּ֛י חֲתַ֥ן בֵּית־אַחְאָ֖ב הֽוּא
27.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since he was a son-in-law of the house of Ahab, he walked in the way of the house of Ahab, and he did evil in the eyes of Yahweh, like the house of Ahab]
See how you translated the same expression in 8:18. Alternate translation: [the kings in the dynasty of Ahab]

Ahaziah’s father Jehoram had married a daughter of Ahab. Your language may have its own term or expression for this relationship. Alternate translation: [he was a relative by marriage of the family of Ahab] or [he was a grandson of Ahab]

28.note: In this context, the word **struck** means “wounded.” Alternate translation: [but the Arameans wounded Joram]

29.note: The expression **to be healed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [to recuperate]

The name **Ramah** is a shortened form of the name Ramoth Gilead, which the author uses in the previous verse. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use the full form of the name here. Alternate translation: [Ramoth Gilead]

29.q: וַ⁠אֲחַזְיָ֨הוּ בֶן־יְהוֹרָ֜ם מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֗ה יָרַ֡ד לִ⁠רְא֞וֹת אֶת־יוֹרָ֧ם בֶּן־אַחְאָ֛ב בְּ⁠יִזְרְעֶ֖אל כִּֽי־חֹלֶ֥ה הֽוּא
29.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because Joram, the son of Ahab, had been wounded, Ahaziah, the son of Jehoram, the king of Judah, went down to see him in Jezreel]
See how you translated the similar expression “go up” in 1:3. Alternate translation: [And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram, the king of Judah, went]
